tagline: From the Blue Ridge crossing to curves through the Rockfish Valley.
intro: US 250 climbs the Blue Ridge as Rockfish Gap Turnpike, while Route 6 curves down Afton Mountain toward the Rockfish Valley. Route 6 carries Virginia Byway status from Avon eastward to SR 650 near Manakin. Virginia’s byway designation identifies scenic roads that introduce travelers to alternative destinations. The valley stretch shares Route 151 before turning along the Rockfish River, then briefly joins four-lane US 29 between mountains.

The older Three Notch’d Road crossed the Blue Ridge at Jarmans Gap, reaching from the future site of Richmond to the Shenandoah Valley by the 1730s. Much of US 250 between Short Pump and Crozet follows that route. Carriages could cross at Rockfish Gap by 1782. At Rockfish Gap, an early-20th-century road received the US 250 designation in 1935; I-64 followed across the mountain in 1972 and 1973.

Start west of Charlottesville on Ivy Road, crossing the Mechums River before climbing toward Rockfish Gap. Route 6 branches off about a mile east of the gap, descending through Afton to Avon and the Rockfish Valley. Continue along the Rockfish River, cross the railway at Faber, and pass through the gap between Shiloh and Butler mountains toward Esmont. The terrain gentles on the approach to Scottsville.

moments.title: Rockfish Gap
moments.text: At about 1,900 feet, Rockfish Gap connects the Piedmont with the Shenandoah Valley. US 250 and I-64 cross here, and the Appalachian Trail passes through the gap. Skyline Drive and the Blue Ridge Parkway meet just north of it. Railway engineers took a different approach: Claudius Crozet oversaw construction of a tunnel beneath the gap in the 1850s. The Chesapeake and Ohio Railway replaced that tunnel on a different alignment in the mid-20th century. The gap also divides drainage: streams on its southeast side flow toward the James, while those to the northwest enter the Shenandoah River system.

moments.title: Faber
moments.text: Route 6 crosses the railway at Faber before entering Albemarle County between Shiloh and Butler mountains. The Waltons mentioned this Nelson County community in several episodes. The drama drew on the geography of Faber and nearby Schuyler for its rural Virginia setting.

moments.title: Esmont
moments.text: Esmont grew on land purchased from the former plantation estate whose name it took. It developed as a farming community with a predominantly African American population. The community was populated in the eighteenth century, but its post office did not arrive until the later nineteenth century. Quarrying added another livelihood: slate extraction began nearby in 1883, and the quarry operation ended in the 1960s. At its peak, the town had a Chesapeake and Ohio Railway depot, three stores, a church and a bank. The bank building was converted into a post office, giving a former financial institution another role in town life.
